headline: A conference study found that four AI chatbots failed to advise emergency care in about 41% of simulated digestive-health emergencies described in Vietnamese, against 15% in English.
score_reason: Pool score 6, lowered by 1: the headline reads as a general finding, but the facts show a conference abstract with simulated cases, four unnamed chatbots and no peer review.
importance_line: Patients who ask chatbots about symptoms in a language other than English, and the hospitals adding chatbots to patient portals, are the people affected, but the test used made-up cases and shows no real patient harm.
summary: Medical Daily reports on a study abstract presented at the American College of Gastroenterology's 2026 meeting in Nashville, which tested four large language models (the AI systems behind chatbots) on simulated digestive-health emergencies in the seven most common languages spoken in the US and found they failed to recommend emergency care far more often in Vietnamese than in English. It is a conference abstract using made-up cases rather than real patients, it has not been peer reviewed, and the four models were not named, so it points to a gap that needs testing, not to harm that has happened.
notes: Full text read. First reported 14 Oct 2026; the exact presentation date within the 9 to 14 Oct meeting is not given, so treated as new. The researcher quoted is only described as the abstract's listed author contact, with no organisation given, so no name is printed.
